items.title: In a first, US set to stay away from UN review of its human rights record
items.summary: The United States is set Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council , accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn’t uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council’s mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe. The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind. It did not. “(W)e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. “This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the spokesperson said, alleging the council’s “persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators.” The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward. As part of such reviews, national delegations — which at times can include a dozen officials or more — make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It’s supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the U.S. snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries — many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors — to follow suit. items.title: With or without authority? The email controversy at Bombay High Court [Watch Video]
items.summary: The Bombay High Court on October 29 quashed an administrative directive that froze trustee appointments to the Shree Saptashrungi Niwasini Devi Trust in Nashik, Maharashtra A division bench comprising Justices GS Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale ruled that District Judge Anju Shende, former Special Officer to then-Chief Justice Shree Chandrashekhar, acted with gross impropriety by issuing an administrative email that halted the lawful selection process. The Court rejected Shende’s defense that she had merely relayed oral orders passed by the Chief Justice. It held that an unverified email cannot usurp judicial authority or stall statutory proceedings without the written approval of the judge. Justices GS Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale In this freewheeling chat, Bar and Bench's Neha Joshi and Mural Krishnan discuss what triggered the controversy, who sent the email, what the officer said to the Court and what the Court eventually held. items.title: Madras High Court calls for more special courts to tackle pending corruption cases in State
items.summary: The Madras High Court has directed the Tamil Nadu government to examine the need for establishing additional special courts to try corruption cases after taking note of the pendency of cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act across the State [A Shahul Hameed v. State of Tamil Nadu and Others]. Justice B Pugalendhi of the Madurai Bench observed that corruption cases could not be treated as an additional responsibility of principal district and sessions judges, particularly when the law contemplated their expeditious disposal. " The pendency of 2,423 cases throughout the State, as on 30.06.2026, cannot be viewed as an ordinary workload to be dealt with as an additional responsibility by the Principal District and Sessions Judges ," the Court said. The Court noted that exclusive special courts under the Prevention of Corruption Act were functioning in only eight districts of Tamil Nadu. In the remaining 30 districts, corruption cases were being heard by principal district and sessions judges alongside their regular judicial and administrative responsibilities. Justice B Pugalendhi The order was passed on a petition filed by A Shahul Hameed, an accused facing trial under the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Indian Penal Code. While considering the petition, the High Court examined whether the existing judicial infrastructure was sufficient to comply with Section 4(4) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The provision requires corruption trials to be conducted on a day-to-day basis, as far as practicable, with an endeavour to conclude proceedings within two years. The Court observed that merely directing trial courts to dispose of cases within two years would not achieve the statutory objective unless adequate infrastructure and personnel were provided. " The very purpose of such a mandate would be defeated if the Courts entrusted with these cases are unable to devote the requisite time and attention to them on account of their other judicial and administrative responsibilities ," it said. The Court noted that a proposal was already pending before the High Court administration to designate additional sessions courts as Special Courts under the Act. Describing the proposal as a welcome step, it directed the Registrar General to pursue the matter. The State government was directed to examine the need for additional special courts, provide necessary infrastructure and supporting staff, and ensure adequate prosecuting personnel. items.title: Five days for some, five years for others: What the Collegium's own record says
items.summary: Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul's memoir, entitled Without Fear or Favour, has started a debate. The former judge said that ex-Chief Justice of India DY Chandrachud was too deferential to the government on appointments . He recalled a Collegium meeting where, he says, the Chief Justice took him aside and wondered whether to phone the government to check its view on a name. Chandrachud has responded that he has not read the book. He says the meetings were respectful, that Kaul never recorded a dissent and that the government has a legitimate role in appointments. We will never see the minutes of that meeting. But we can look at something else: the dates. Every Collegium recommendation has a date. So does every government notification. If names are being settled with the government before the Collegium meets, the government has little reason to sit on them afterwards and the gap between the two dates should shrink. Between October 2017 - when the Collegium began putting its resolutions online - and October 2026, 63 judges were recommended for Supreme Court elevation in 24 rounds. For each judge, I noted the date of the Collegium's resolution and the date on which the government notified the appointment. Here's what the numbers reveal. The government's varying speed Across all 63 judges, the usual wait was seven days. But that figure hides two very different periods. Before 2023, the government often took its time. Indu Malhotra waited 106 days. KM Joseph waited 205 days. His name was sent back and when he was finally appointed, he was placed below two judges who had been recommended months after him. Dipankar Datta waited 76 days. Five judges recommended in December 2022 waited 53 days. From January 2023, the picture changes completely. 28 judges were recommended in 13 rounds and not one waited more than 10 days. The usual wait fell to five days. I ran standard statistical tests on these figures (a Mann–Whitney test gives p = 0.004) and the drop is far too large to be put down to chance. The turning point is easy to find. On February 3, 2023, a bench of Justices Kaul and AS Oka was hearing a contempt case about delays in appointments. Justice Kaul pointed out that five names sent in December were still pending. items.title: Calcutta High Court declines urgent relief in plea alleging fake encounter threat to Sumit Roy
items.summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday declined to urgently intervene in a plea alleging that the State police forced Sumit Roy, close aide of Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Abhishek Banerjee, to confess that he had stored around ₹1.02 crore seized by the police at the party's former office in Diamond Harbour [Susmita Ghosh v. State of West Bengal and Ors.]. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya directed that the petition filed by Sumit Roy's wife, Sushmita Ghosh, be listed after the ongoing court vacation. The Court noted that Ghosh has approached it seeking protection for her husband and expressing apprehension that he might be falsely implicated in the case. It also recorded the State government's submission that the matter was still under investigation. "State is represented by Mr. Mitra who is the Learned Advocate General who has submitted that husband of the petitioner is already in custody and investigation is going on. In view of the aforesaid, let the matter appear before the regular bench after reopening," the Court said. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya Ghosh alleged that her husband, who is currently in police custody, was threatened with a fake encounter to make him confess that he had stored crores of rupees at the premises. According to the plea, Roy was recently taken to the premises, where he saw police officials arranging and counting bundles of currency notes. He was then forced to wear a black mask and pose before the cash while the Additional Superintendent of Police (Zonal) addressed a press conference claiming a seizure of the amount, the plea said. The plea alleged that various criminal proceedings were initiated against Roy only after the change of government in West Bengal on May 4, as part of a political vendetta aimed at targeting TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee. Ghosh urged the Court to constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) comprising independent police officers, under the supervision of a retired Calcutta High Court judge, to investigate allegations of custodial intimidation, fabrication and planting of evidence, and coercion to obtain confessional statements. Advocate Biswaroop Bhattacharyya appeared for the petitioner. The State was represented by Advocate General Surojit Nath Mitra .

items.summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) told the Delhi High Court that it received a “grave and serious” objection to registering ‘Waris Punjab De’ as a political party, stating that it could adversely affect the “sovereignty and integrity of India." Waris Punjab, meaning ‘Heirs of Punjab’, was founded by actor-activist Deep Sidhu in 2021. Jailed pro-Khalistan Member of Parliament (MP) Amritpal Singh now heads it. The organisation plans to contest the Punjab Assembly elections due in early 2027. The ECI said that on July 9, 2026, it received a “very sensitive input” alleging that Waris Punjab De is “rooted in separatism”, was founded by individuals detained under the National Security Act (NSA) and “poses grave concerns regarding its allegiance to sovereignty and integrity of India”. It said that while the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) of Punjab gave a positive verification report about the organisation on April 27, 2026, the objection about its separatist roots was received in July 2026, and the CEO was then instructed to conduct a "comprehensive background inquiry." The report of this inquiry is awaited, the ECI said. It made the disclosure in two separate affidavits, dated September 14, 2026, and November 3, 2026. They came in response to a writ petition by Waris Punjab De seeking an expeditious decision on its application seeking registration. In its September 14 affidavit, the ECI stated that Waris Punjab De submitted the application for registration on January 22, 2025, and the same was acknowledged by the Commission on February 6, 2025. After scrutiny, a deficiency letter was issued to the applicant on September 10, 2025, and the next day, the ECI requested the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) of Punjab to initiate the verification process. The affidavit adds that two reminders were sent to the CEO, Punjab – on March 18, 2026, and April 20, 2026 – to expedite the field verification process. The CEO of Punjab submitted a “positive verification report” on April 27, 2026, and the report was under active consideration. items.title: Possibility of crime no ground to restrict operating hours of licensed bars: Kerala High Court
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Tuesday held that the Police cannot impose restrictions on the timings of DJ parties conducted by establishments with appropriate liquor licences (FL-3 permits) that allow their operation during extended hours [ Mahadevan v State of Kerala & ors ]. Justice Murali Purushothaman opined that the mere possibility of criminal activities is no ground to impose restrictions on the operation of such facilities. " Mere possibility of criminal activities cannot, by itself, constitute sufficient justification for imposing restrictions under the Kerala Police Act on the extended operating hours of FL3 hotels permitted under the Foreign Liquor Amendment Rules," the Court said. The Court held that while the Police have a responsibility to curb crime, it cannot restrict the activities of licenced bars by merely citing suspicions of criminal activities like drug use at such premises, unless rules restricting such bar timings are put in place by the State. "If the police have reason to believe that criminal activities are taking place under the guise of DJ parties in hotels, it is the responsibility of the police to take stringent action in accordance with law to curb the same...Until the government frames appropriate rules prescribing exception to the extended hours of operation permitted in the Foreign Liquor Rules, the police cannot curtail or restrict the operating hours of the hotel contrary to the provisions granted under those Rules in the absence of special grounds justifying such restrictions, " the Court held. items.title: No plans to allot Central Secretariat Club premises to anyone at this stage: Centre to Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Central government has informed the Delhi High Court that there is no proposal to allot the Central Secretariat Club premises to anyone at this stage. Central Government Standing Counsel (CGSC) Radhika Bishwajit Dubey made the statement before Justice Amit Mahajan on November 5 during the hearing of an application filed by the Club seeking stay on the government’s order of de-recognition and eviction of the club. “Ms Radhika Bishwajit Dubey, learned CGSC for the respondents, on instructions, submits that there is no proposal to allot the subject premises to any party at this stage. Considering the above, no order is required to be passed. The petitioners are permitted to take away their belongings in next one week,” the Court said in its order. The case will be heard next on December 21. Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court The application was filed by the Club in its already pending case challenging the de-recognition and the eviction order. It stated that the government was in the process of handing over possession of the land to RML Hospital, "thereby confronting this Hon’ble Court with a completed fait accompli" before its petition could be heard. On March 3, the allotment of the land to the Club was cancelled by the Central government’s Directorate of Estates. On July 14, the Club was de-recognised by the Union Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievance and Pensions citing constant violations and prima facie evidence of illegitimate and untoward activities. The de-recognition order stated that the Club consistently failed to maintain a meaningful and representative membership base of Central government employees in service. The order stated that the Club's executive committee is involved in harbouring unauthorised occupants in illegal possession and encroachment of government property. Further, it also stated that there is no legally constituted management committee to run the affairs of the club. On July 17, the Directorate of Estates issued an eviction notice, directing immediate vacation of the Club from the property. The Club moved the Court challenging both the orders before the High Court. Diya Kapur Senior Advocate Diya Kapur with advocates Akhil Sachhar, Nakul Gandhi, Darshit Sidhabatti, Anushka Khaitan, Raghav Kumar, Shruti Jain and Naibedya Dash appeared for Central Secretariat Club. items.title: Bombay High Court quashes Customs order flagged for citing non-existent AI-generated judgments
items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently set aside a customs department order after taking note of concerns that the adjudicating authority had relied on non-existent, artificial intelligence (AI) generated Supreme Court judgments [ Quanta Logistics Pvt Ltd v. Commissioner of Customs (Import-I) ]. A Bench of Justices MS Karnik and Sandesh D Patil quashed an August 11, 2026 order passed by the customs commissioner against Quanta Logistics. Justice MS Karnik, Justice Sandesh Patil Quanta argued that the customs authority passed the order by resorting to AI without an independent application of mind. Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond demonstrated that the order cited two Supreme Court judgments that did not exist in any database, describing them as possible AI hallucinations. When Quanta requested for copies of the cited judgment, the department failed to provide the same. Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond The petitioner relied on the 2026 Supreme Court decision in Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v. Union of India, in which the apex court had emphasised on a "zero-tolerance" approach to tackling the use of AI-generated precedents without due verification. In response, the Customs department agreed that the order under challenge could be quashed and the matter reconsidered. Consequently, the High Court quashed the Customs order by consent and directed the petitioner to appear before the authority so that the matter can be examined afresh. In a similar ruling on October 28, 2026, the same Bench quashed an order against Asahi India Glass Ltd. [Asahi India Glass Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner of Customs Group III & Anr.] The adjudicating authority relied on untraceable judicial precedents to treat the fifteen-day statutory limit under Section 17(5) as directory. In its affidavit, the department admitted that the citations could not be traced in the form given and profusely regretted the error. The High Court remitted the case for fresh adjudication within four weeks, directing adherence to prior binding classification. Dhond appeared along with advocates Bimal Rajasekhar and Sunand Subramaniam for Quanta. Senior advocate Balbir Singh with advocates Jitendra Singh, Anshuman Sahni, Rahul Gupta and Amir Arsiwala appeared for Asahi India Glass. Senior Advocate Balbir Singh Advocates Jitendra B Mishra, Sangeeta Yadav, Maya Majumdar, Megha Bajoria and Khushi P Agarwal appeared for the customs department. items.title: Library book procurement scam: Madras HC tells DVAC to file FIR
items.summary: A contempt of court petition was filed before the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Tuesday, November 10, alleging disobedience of a June 2024 order that directed the Tamil Nadu government to ensure transparency in the procurement of books for public libraries. Hearing the matter, a Bench of Justices GR Swaminathan and MD Sumathi directed the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) to register an FIR into alleged fraudulent practices and sought the names of officials responsible for the procurement irregularities. Justice GR Swaminathan, who was part of the Bench that passed the original order along with Justice R Mahadevan (now a Supreme Court judge), told the newly appointed Director of Public Libraries, RV Shajeevana, that the matters that had recently come to light amounted to "blatant disobedience" of the court's directions. The judge said the Bench intended to take the matter very seriously. The judges said the fraudulent practices in the procurement of books for public libraries had been uncovered following an article written by Tamil author Perumal Murugan. Justice Swaminathan said that "heads must roll" over the alleged scam and sought to know who had recommended the procurement of publications by Agal Vilakku. "Don't try to save anybody," Justice Swaminathan told the Director of Public Libraries, while questioning why action had not been taken against those responsible. The judge observed that if the director had lodged a complaint in 2024 and an FIR had been registered then, the alleged scam that has now come to light could have been prevented. The Bench directed the Director of Public Libraries to submit, by the following day, a list of officials responsible for the fraudulent procurement so that contempt proceedings could be initiated against them. Justice Swaminathan also sought the names of all officials involved and directed that the bank accounts of the publishers allegedly involved in the irregularities be seized. Additional Advocate General B Saravanan told the court that all details would be placed before it within 24 hours. State Public Prosecutor R John Sathyan informed the Bench that the DVAC had received a complaint from the School Education Department on November 6, 2026, and commenced a detailed inquiry into the issue on November 7. items.title: ‘Like a knight hopping on chessboard’: What Maythil Radhakrishnan is to his readers
items.summary: It is hard to explain why a writer like Maythil Radhakrishnan, who qualifies to be a nerd, matters. Description falls short of the experience of reading him, and the most honest way to introduce his work is to put a book in someone's hands. Recently, when he was announced the winner of the Ezhuthachan Award, the highest honour given to a Malayalam writer by the Government of Keralam, Maythil’s readers were overjoyed and superlative in the praise of their beloved author. One sentiment that kept coming up was that he was grossly underrated; a writer belatedly recognised by a state for his literary genius. Maythil, 82, who wrote stories in his college years and had a stint in journalism, eventually chose the path of technology, as head of the computer department at a Norwegian shipping company and later, as senior technical writer with the Nest USA’s Chennai branch. Alongside, he wrote novels such as Sooryavamsam , Chuvanna Vidooshakarute Anchampathi and Hitchcockinte Itapetal ; poetry collections such as Bhoomiyeyum Maranatheyum Kurichu ; and, above all, short story collections like Naayakanmaar Shavapetakangalil and Dylan Thomasinte Panth . A native of Palakkad by birth, he grew up in the same terrain as MT Vasudevan Nair, the doyen of Malayalam literature, but slipped away to other shores. What might have taken him further away, from writing and his homeland, was his desire to study filmmaking in the US, for which he was all prepared, until his visa was rejected. Maythil, dejected, fell back to his writing, which, he would say in interviews, was engineering, not aesthetics. Readers may disagree. “It is hyper detailed, he can write about a simple table for 12 pages and you won’t be bored. His language is that unique, it is a sort of poetry that refuses to deal with social issues or personal despair or longing as writers tend to dwell in,” says veteran writer M Mukundan. He compares him to French writer-filmmaker Georges Perec whose writing was once described as one that hops like a knight on a chessboard. “You might say that of Maythil as well, he is hopping about on a chessboard, playing with language in a way only he can, creating worlds of poetry. He gives one image which translates into many in a reader’s mind,” says Mukundan. items.title: CM Naidu says TDP will study if ‘forced conversions’ affected AP civic poll results
items.summary: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister and Telugu Desam Party chief N Chandrababu Naidu has said his party will examine whether alleged forced religious conversions played a role in the ruling coalition’s losses in some constituencies in the recent local body elections. The TDP president addressed the media on November 9 to announce the TDP–Jana Sena Party–Bharatiya Janata Party coalition’s sweeping victory in elections to urban local bodies, Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituencies (ZPTCs) and Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituencies (MPTCs). Reflecting on the coalition’s losses in a few places, including Anantapur and tribal districts such as Alluri Sitharama Raju, Chandrababu Naidu said: “I have said in the past that forcible conversions have happened. This needs to be studied, whether people did any deliberate mischief after forcible conversions.” Leaders of the three coalition parties have frequently accused the opposition YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) of enabling forced religious conversions during YS Jagan Mohan Reddy’s tenure as Chief Minister. Jagan is a practising Christian. But they have not provided evidence to support the allegations. Chandrababu Naidu said that the party would conduct a comprehensive review of its losses in certain areas. He cited the government’s work in tribal regions, including promoting Araku Coffee internationally and implementing development plans, but said the expected electoral results had not materialised. He said the party would analyse the results and examine whether voters had been “swayed” by any form of “inducement”. “How can the entire state go one way, and just one or two constituencies go the other way? If public sentiment differs, we will work together with them. If they are being deceived, then we will control that,” Chandrababu Naidu said. He added that the party would correct any mistakes and take firm action if necessary. Announcing the coalition’s victory in the local body polls, Chandrababu Naidu said its combined vote share had increased since the 2024 Assembly elections, rising from 55.3% to 58.9% in the urban local body elections—an increase of 3.6 percentage points. The YSRCP’s vote share, he said, fell from 39.81% to 33.56%, a decline of 6.25 percentage points. The CM said that the alliance had won 575 of the 659 ZPTC seats statewide and led in 27 of the 28 districts. The YSRCP won more seats than the alliance only in Alluri Sitharama Raju district.
